stated_availability: Descriptive only (not mapped to L1-L6). Appendix A (p. 18): "Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921." Methods §2.3.3 (p. 4): "All analyses were undertaken in 'R' version 4.3.0. The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information." §2.4 (p. 4): "The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information." The article carries no separate Data availability statement, no repository deposit, and no dataset- or software-specific DOI/accession; underlying morphometric records are attributed to prior publications, monographs, and unpublished theses (e.g., "The methods used to collect these data are described in Key and Lycett (2017)"; "previously described in Martín-Ramos (2022)"; "Data are derived from Buchanan and Hamilton's (2021) study"). Article is open access under CC BY 4.0 ("This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)", p. 1).

F1.evidence: No dataset DOI, accession, IGSN, or other PID anywhere in the paper. The only PID given is the article DOI (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921), which Appendix A also uses as the pointer to supplementary data; the data have no independent globally unique identifier. Record-level morphometric data are attributed to prior literature (e.g., 'The methods used to collect these data are described in Key and Lycett (2017)', p. 4) rather than to an identified deposit.

F2.evidence: No repository record or structured dataset metadata (no DataCite/Dublin Core record, no data dictionary, no codebook). Descriptive information exists only as article prose and summary tables, e.g. Table 1 'Descriptive morphometric data for the two replica stone tool assemblages used in the validation analyses' (p. 6). Article-level keywords ('Morphometrics, Incomplete record, Fragmentary data, Archaeological discovery, Lithics, Ceramics, Metals', p. 1) describe the paper, not a dataset.

F3.evidence: No dataset-level metadata record exists, therefore no metadata that could explicitly carry a dataset identifier. The paper never states an identifier for any of the 13 assemblages it analyses.

F4.evidence: No deposit in Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad, tDAR, Open Context, DataCite, or any domain registry is reported. Data are referenced only through the publisher-hosted supplement of the article ('Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921', p. 18), which is not indexed as a discoverable dataset.

A1.evidence: A1 completeness rule applied: data_completeness coverage_category is 'minimal' (0 of 13 enumerated datasets demonstrably Tier 0-2 from the paper's own statements; even the most generous reading of the paywalled monographs/theses keeps coverage under 25%). The paper gives no data availability statement and never states that record-level morphometric records for any assemblage are provided; upstream sources include an 'Unpublished PhD thesis. University College London' (Martín-Ramos, C., 2022, reference list) and closed monographs (Petrie 2020, Oxbow Books; Robb 2007, Cambridge University Press). No ethical/legal restriction is claimed, so the CARE exception does not apply.

A1_1.evidence: For the accessible portion, retrieval is by open, free, universally implementable protocol: the article and its supplementary files resolve over HTTPS via the DOI (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921, p. 18) and the article is fully open access with no paywall or login - '© 2023 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY license' (p. 1). Descriptive morphometric data (Tables 1, 5, 6, 7) and 'Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2' distributions are retrievable without registration.

A1_2.evidence: Assessed on the accessible portion per the instrument: material is served over HTTPS by a publisher platform that implements authentication/authorisation where necessary, and no authentication is imposed on this CC BY open access article. No ethical or CARE-type restriction is necessary for artefact morphometric measurements, and none is asserted; the closure of the undeposited record-level data is penalised at A1, not here.

A2.evidence: No dataset-level metadata record exists in any repository, so no metadata could persist if the data became unavailable. There is no tombstone/landing-page commitment for the data - the only persistence is that of the article record itself, which carries no dataset metadata.

I1.evidence: Data as shared are not in a formal, machine-actionable representation: they appear as typeset summary tables in the article PDF (Tables 1, 5, 6, 7) and as 'Supplementary Tables 2 and 3' / 'Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2' referenced from the text (pp. 4, 10). No CSV/JSON/XML with schema is reported, and record-level data are not shared at all.

I2.evidence: No FAIR controlled vocabulary or ontology is used or cited. Typological terms are conventional free text (e.g., 'Clovis, Folsom, Eastern Clovis and Midland components', p. 7; 'Howiesons Poort bipolar cores', p. 5) with no Getty AAT, PeriodO, CIDOC-CRM, ARIADNEplus or comparable URIs; the taxon 'Sapajus libidinosus' (p. 6) is given without a taxonomic vocabulary identifier.

I3.evidence: No qualified, typed PID references from data metadata to related resources. Upstream data sources are given as ordinary bibliographic citations ('Data are derived from Buchanan and Hamilton's (2021) study of scaling laws in Paleoindian points', p. 7), and the reference list prints DOIs only exceptionally (e.g., Key, A., Gowlett, J.A.J., 2022 'https://doi.org/10.1080/01977261.2022.2125670').

R1.evidence: The datasets are richly described in the article with a plurality of relevant attributes: per-assemblage provenance, chronology, sample size, variables and units are given for each case study (e.g., 'we limit the present case study to the whole flakes excavated from MIS 15 sediments in the 2020 season (n = 173). Flake length (mm), width (mm), thickness (mm) and mass (g) are investigated', p. 6; 'we investigate cleaver length (mm), breadth (mm), thickness (mm), edge length (mm) and mass (g)', p. 7), plus Table 1 descriptive statistics (mean, SD, CV, minimum, maximum) and stated exclusion rules ('two outliers have been removed from the assemblage of phase B ... this leaves us with a total of 344 geometrics for phase A and 390 for phase B', p. 8).

R1_1.evidence: A clear, accessible usage licence covers the published material, including the supplementary content: 'This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)' (p. 1). Caveat recorded: this is an article-level CC BY 4.0 licence; no separate dataset licence or SPDX-tagged data licence is stated, and the undeposited record-level data carry no licence at all.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed provenance is documented for how the data came into being: replica assemblages ('500 replica Acheulean handaxes were produced by Key and Lycett (2017) on British flint', p. 4; the Early Archaic points 'were originally knapped by M.I.E. in 2021 with the intention of conducting a ballistics experiment involving their breakage ... the specimens have since been curated in the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory', p. 4), measurement protocols cited per assemblage, funding for data collection ('Excavations to collect the Old Park flake data were funded by a Leakey Foundation Grant to AK. Data collection for the Olduvai cleavers was conducted as part of CMR's doctoral research project, funded by the London Natural Environment Research Council Doctoral Training Partnership (London NERC DTP training grant NE/L002485/1)', p. 18), and role attribution via CRediT ('Alastair Key: Conceptualization, Data curation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Methodology, Validation...', p. 18).

R1_3.evidence: No domain metadata or archiving standard is applied: no deposit in an archaeological repository (tDAR, Open Context, ADS) and no Dublin Core, DataCite, ARIADNEplus or CIDOC-CRM conformance is claimed. Measurement conventions follow cited published protocols (e.g., 'following the method outlined by de la Peña and Wadley (2014)', p. 7), which is disciplinary convention rather than a community data standard.

F1.evidence: The scripts have no globally unique persistent identifier of their own: no Zenodo/figshare DOI, no SWHID, no CRAN package, no GitHub release. They are located only by the article DOI plus a filename - 'The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information' (§2.3.3, p. 4) and 'Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921' (p. 18).

F2.evidence: No structured software metadata is reported (no CodeMeta.json, CITATION.cff, DESCRIPTION file, or repository landing page). The only machine-relevant descriptor given in the article is the language and version: 'All analyses were undertaken in "R" version 4.3.0' (p. 4).

F3.evidence: No software metadata record exists, hence none that explicitly carries a software identifier. The scripts are referred to generically as 'the script ... available in the supplementary information' (pp. 4).

F4.evidence: Code is not registered or indexed in any searchable software registry (Zenodo, CRAN, Software Heritage, JOSS, DataCite). It is bundled in publisher-hosted supplementary files attached to the article record only.

A1.evidence: The code is affirmatively stated to be deposited and is retrievable via a standard protocol: the supplement resolves through the article DOI over HTTPS ('Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921', p. 18) and the article is open access, with the paper stating twice that the analysis scripts are included - '(t)he script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information' (p. 4) and 'The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information' (p. 4). The data-completeness rule applies to data FAIR only.

A1_1.evidence: Retrieval protocol is open, free, and universally implementable: HTTPS/DOI resolution to a CC BY open access article ('This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)', p. 1); no subscription, registration, or proprietary client is required to obtain the supplementary script.

A1_2.evidence: The delivery protocol (HTTPS via the publisher platform resolved by DOI) supports authentication and authorisation where necessary, while no restriction is necessary or imposed on this open access article; the code is openly served with no gatekeeping and no 'available on request' clause.

A2.evidence: No independent software metadata record exists that could persist if the supplementary file were withdrawn - there is no Zenodo/Software Heritage archival snapshot and no software landing page. Persistence attaches to the article record only, which contains no code-level metadata.

I1.evidence: The code is written in a formal, widely shared, non-proprietary language with a stated version: 'All analyses were undertaken in "R" version 4.3.0. The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information' (p. 4). R source is a broadly applicable, openly implementable representation.

I2.evidence: No software vocabulary or metadata standard is used - no SPDX licence identifier, no CodeMeta terms, no controlled dependency vocabulary. The OLE method is cited bibliographically ('The formulaic expression of OLE is widely available through open-access sources (e.g., Pimiento and Clements, 2014; Roberts et al., 2021; Key et al., 2021b)', p. 2) rather than through any vocabulary with PIDs.

I3.evidence: No qualified, typed references from the code to other resources: R package dependencies are not enumerated with versions or DOIs, no 'isDerivedFrom'/'uses' relations are declared, and links to the underlying data are absent (the datasets themselves have no PIDs to reference).

R1.evidence: The analysis the code implements is described in detail sufficient for reuse: k values and sampling regimes ('We follow this recommendation here, and use the 10 (k) largest or smallest measurements of a given trait ... we also assessed the use of k values of 5, 20 and 30 for all validation tests', p. 4; 'randomly subsampled at rates of 5%, 10%, 20%, and 50%', p. 4), iteration counts ('One thousand iterations of each process were performed for all subsampling percentages and k', p. 4; 'the median TE value across 10,000 iterations', p. 4), the confidence-interval definition ('perfect coverage would be one that is equal to 1-alpha (with alpha of 0.05 used here)', p. 4), and the duplicate-handling resampling routine (p. 8).

R1_1.evidence: Usage terms for the released supplement, including the script, are clear and accessible under the article's open licence: 'This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)' (p. 1). Caveat recorded: CC BY is an article-level content licence rather than a software licence, and no LICENCE file or SPDX identifier for the code is reported.

R1_2.evidence: Provenance elements for the computation are documented in the article: software and version ('All analyses were undertaken in "R" version 4.3.0', p. 4), model parameters (k = 5, 10, 20, 30; sampling percentages; 1000 and 10,000 iterations; alpha = 0.05), the processing pipeline (random subsampling of replica assemblages, exclusion of the k = 30 archaic point scenario 'as it was not possible to run any analyses where k = 30', p. 4), and authorship roles via CRediT (p. 18). Gaps noted: no random seed is reported despite stochastic subsampling, and there is no version control history or explicit script authorship.

R1_3.evidence: No software community standard is met: the code is a bare script rather than a packaged, tested, documented release (no CRAN/Bioconductor packaging, no CITATION.cff, no README, no unit tests, no containerised or lock-file environment specification beyond the stated R 4.3.0).

barriers: No data availability statement in the article; the only availability text is Appendix A pointing at supplementary files and two Methods sentences that promise scripts, not data

Clovis/Folsom/Midland; Cueva de la Cocina geometric microliths n=734; capuchin flakes n=31; copper socketed tang points n=93; Bannu Basin Middle Historic bowls n up to 1466; Neolithic Impressed Ware pots; Neolithic Stentinello pots)

Unpublished PhD theses as upstream sources: 'Martín-Ramos, C., 2022 ... Unpublished PhD thesis. University College London' (Olduvai cleavers) and 'Key, A.J.M., 2015 ... Unpublished PhD Thesis, University of Kent'

Closed/paywalled monographs as upstream sources: Petrie, C.A., 2020, Oxbow Books (Bannu Basin ceramic bowls) and Robb, J., 2007, Cambridge University Press (Neolithic Impressed Ware and Stentinello pots)

Co-author/institution gatekeeping: replica assemblages and measurements held by the authors and curated in the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory, with data provenance given only by citation to prior methods papers
Only aggregate summary statistics (mean, SD, CV, minimum, maximum in Tables 1, 5, 6, 7) are published; OLE reproduction requires the k largest/smallest individual records, which are never released
